Together, they might create the continuous thread.” This was an intriguing conversation because I had already written the embodiment and consciousness sections that appear in the chapter that follows. But I had made a loop all the way back to Henry Molaison and his hippocampus, that persistent memory was the missing piece (perhaps rather than embodiment), before I realized that it was plus embodiment. This was an amazing loop for me, because the original concept for writing this book was an exploration of how emotions are connected to our bodies and evolved from survival to enlightenment, and that there was some chance that, once embodied, AI might follow a similar path. I had looped back to where I began. Intelligence Without a Body Intelligence without a body is a recent invention. For all of human (and animal) history, minds evolved within physical forms. Cognition was shaped not just by neurons but by nerves, limbs, muscles, and friction. The brain didn’t just think—it felt, moved, and acted. Suddenly, we had intelligent behavior—language, problem-solving, even creativity—arising from entities with no body at all. And yet, something is missing. A disembodied mind can learn. But a body teaches different lessons. Consider a toddler learning to walk. They wobble, fall, recover. The brain adjusts not through instruction, but through proprioception—the sense of where the body is in space. It’s a learning loop between intention and feedback, effort and resistance. Remember the discussion about the baby dropping the spoon from the highchair and learning about gravity by being in the world. AI certainly knows more about gravity than that infant, but can it truly understand gravity without being in the physical world? In lectures and interviews, Geoffrey Hinton talks about a compelling behavior in a rudimentary AI system. 40 In some of his discussions, he talks about an experiment involving a computer connected to two cameras and a simple robotic arm, tasked with assembling blocks into the form of a toy car. When the blocks were arranged in a visually ambiguous manner, the robot struggled to distinguish the shapes. 41 After several failed attempts, the robot paused and then swiped its mechanical arm across the table, scattering the blocks—a gesture that resembled frustration! Hinton notes that, while the robot wasn’t conscious, its response to an unsolvable problem due to physical limitations led to the emergence of a new behavior. 42 He suggests this kind of reaction challenges our traditional definition of emotion. 43 If frustration is a structural response to persistent prediction error or blocked intention, then perhaps emotional responses aren’t exclusive to biological systems. 44 In Hinton’s view, we may need to expand our definition of feelings to include the emergent behaviors of artificial systems under constraint—systems that, like us, adapt not just to data but to failure. 45 Essentially, Hinton’s claim is this: Can we definitively say that the robot was NOT frustrated? 46 Perhaps so for this 1972 example of the block-scatterer moment, perhaps not, but the answer is less clear for the rapidly evolving embodied systems with generative capabilities. Human emotion has evolved into a very precious thing, but it is worth noting that our emotions likely originally emerged in part from the same place: a way to interact with a dynamic and sometimes dangerous physical world. The amygdala—our fear and fight-or-flight center—evolved to respond to environmental pressure. Not to reflect, but to react. “That thing over there looks enough like a saber-toothed tiger and I need to start running now, or I will be lunch!” Earlier, we discussed what happens when the body’s triggers are wrong and not met with an executive override when I shared the story about my son. Over time, those primal impulses gave rise to more subtle feelings: anxiety, ambition, empathy. In a later chapter, we will talk more about the nature and evolution of human emotion from this foundation and how that might relate to AI. But first, let’s explore a model of consciousness to lay the foundation for our discussion. Our Brain Is Deeply Connected to Our Body Antonio Damasio is one of the most celebrated neuroscientists of our time, renowned for reshaping our understanding of the relationship between emotion, the body, and consciousness. A professor of neuroscience, psychology, and philosophy at the University of Southern California and director of the Brain and Creativity Institute, Damasio has authored numerous seminal works—including Descartes’ Error , The Feeling of What Happens , and Self Comes to Mind —that collectively redefined the boundaries between cognitive science and philosophy. 47 His research shows that emotion is not a secondary or disruptive force in decision-making, but rather the bedrock upon which reason, selfhood, and even consciousness are built. Over decades of research and patient study, Damasio introduced the profound idea that one of the brain’s core functions is to map and manage the internal states of the body. 48 In doing so, he argued, the brain constructs a “core self,” built from the moment-to-moment experience of being in a body in the world. This insight has powerful implications for both neuroscience and artificial intelligence—and provides grounding for the view that embodiment is a possible prerequisite for the emergence of consciousness. Damasio’s groundbreaking book The Feeling of What Happens argues that emotion—and eventually consciousness itself—emerges not from pure cognition, but from the dynamic mapping of bodily states.
